procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court in Himachal Pradesh (inferred, as the High Court heard a Criminal Appeal)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.06.2014 of the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla in Criminal Appeal No. 404 of 2009.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla, issued a Judgment and Order on 26.06.2014 in Criminal Appeal No. 404 of 2009.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Shafhi Mohammad filed a Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 2302 of 2017 in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court heard arguments on the admissibility of electronic records, as an identical question arose in the petition. The Court appointed amicus curiae and also heard counsel for the Union of India.

issue.issue_text: Whether the requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is mandatory for the admissibility of electronic evidence when the person producing it is not in possession or control of the original device.

law.point: The requirement to furnish a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is a procedural rule.
text_reference: It was submitted that Section 65B of the Evidence Act was a procedural provision...
The applicability of requirement of certificate being procedural can be relaxed by Court wherever interest of justice so justifies.

law.point: This procedural requirement applies only when the person producing the electronic evidence is in control of the original device and is in a position to produce the certificate.
text_reference: The applicability of procedural requirement under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act of furnishing certificate is to be applied only when such electronic evidence is produced by a person who is in a position to produce such certificate being in control of the said device and not of the opposite party.

law.point: When a party is not in possession of the original device, the general provisions for proving secondary evidence under Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act can be invoked.
text_reference: In a case where electronic evidence is produced by a party who is not in possession of a device, applicability of Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act cannot be held to be excluded. In such case, procedure under the said Sections can certainly be invoked.

application.point: The Court reasoned that a party who does not possess or control the device from which an electronic document was generated cannot be expected to produce a certificate under Section 65B(4).
text_reference: Such party cannot be required to produce certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act.

application.point: To mandatorily require a certificate in such a situation would lead to a denial of justice, as it would prevent a party from presenting authentic and relevant evidence simply because they cannot fulfill an impossible procedural step.
text_reference: If this is not so permitted, it will be denial of justice to the person who is in possession of authentic evidence/witness but on account of manner of proving, such document is kept out of consideration by the court in absence of certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act, which party producing cannot possibly secure.

application.point: Therefore, the court can relax the requirement for a certificate in the interest of justice and allow the admissibility of the electronic evidence to be determined through other means.
text_reference: The applicability of requirement of certificate being procedural can be relaxed by Court wherever interest of justice so justifies.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is not always mandatory. It is not required when the person producing the electronic evidence is not in possession or control of the original device and is therefore unable to obtain such a certificate. In these circumstances, the court can relax the procedural requirement in the interest of justice, and the party can prove the evidence by invoking other provisions of the Evidence Act, such as Sections 63 and 65.

issue.issue_text: Whether videography of the scene of crime or scene of recovery during investigation should be necessary to inspire confidence in the evidence collected.

facts: The Supreme Court considered the question of whether videography of a crime or recovery scene should be a necessary part of an investigation.
The Union Home Secretary and state Chief Secretaries discussed the matter and decided to form a Committee of Experts (COE) to create a road-map and Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for its use.
Practical concerns were raised regarding the implementation of videography, including scarcity of funds, issues of data security and storage, and the admissibility of such evidence.
The court adjourned the matter to a later date to finalize the road-map and SOP, indicating its ongoing oversight of the implementation process.
law: The court affirmed the principle that the law of evidence should embrace new techniques and devices, provided their accuracy can be proven. Electronic evidence is admissible subject to safeguards regarding its authenticity. (Ram Singh and Others v. Col. Ram Singh)

New technological devices are the 'order of the day,' and while they are susceptible to tampering, evidence from them should not be rejected outright; a stringent standard of proof for authenticity is required. (Tukaram S. Dighole v. Manikrao Shivaji Kokate)
Advancements in information technology and scientific temper must be incorporated into investigation methods. (Tomaso Bruno and Anr. v. State of Uttar Pradesh)

The requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act for the admissibility of electronic evidence is not always mandatory. This procedural requirement can be relaxed by the court in the interest of justice, particularly when the party producing the evidence is not in possession of the device from which it was generated.
application: The court noted the submission by the Additional Solicitor General that videography is a modern technological tool that helps in investigations and is successfully used in other countries, such as the USA and UK, with 'Body-Worn Cameras'.
The court recognized that videography acts as both a deterrent to anti-social behavior and a tool for collecting evidence.
It was pointed out that Indian law already provides for videography in certain contexts, such as under Section 54-A (identification process) and Section 164(1) (confessions) of the Cr.P.C.

By clarifying the law on the admissibility of electronic evidence, particularly by relaxing the strict requirement for a certificate under Section 65B(4), the court removed a potential technical barrier to the use of videography, ensuring that authentic evidence is not excluded from consideration.
The court actively facilitated the implementation of this measure by overseeing the creation of a Committee of Experts to develop a formal road-map and SOP.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that videography of the scene of a crime or recovery should be necessary to inspire confidence in the evidence. The court supported this by affirming the legal principle that new technologies should be embraced in evidence collection, clarifying the rules for the admissibility of electronic evidence to prevent its exclusion on technical grounds, and overseeing the creation of a formal procedure for its implementation in investigations.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is mandatory for the admissibility of electronic evidence when the person producing it is not in possession or control of the original device.
appellant_arguments: The applicability of the procedural requirement under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act of furnishing a certificate is to be applied only when such electronic evidence is produced by a person who is in a position to produce such certificate, being in control of the said device.

In a case where electronic evidence is produced by a party who is not in possession of a device, the applicability of Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act cannot be held to be excluded and the procedure under those sections can be invoked.

If a party not in possession of the original device is still required to produce a certificate, it would be a denial of justice as authentic evidence would be kept out of consideration because the party producing it cannot possibly secure the certificate.
The requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) is not always mandatory.

arguments.issue_text: Whether videography of the scene of crime or scene of recovery during investigation should be necessary to inspire confidence in the evidence collected.

cases.case_name: Tomaso Bruno and Anr. v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: Regarding the admissibility of electronic evidence, the possibility of tampering must be ruled out. While the reliability of the evidence is determined by the facts and circumstances of the case, its threshold admissibility cannot be dismissed on a technicality if it is relevant.

cases.principle: Regarding the admissibility of electronic evidence, the possibility of tampering must be ruled out. While the reliability of the evidence is determined by the facts and circumstances of the case, its threshold admissibility cannot be dismissed on a technicality if it is relevant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A party who is not in possession of the device from which an electronic document is produced cannot be required to produce a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act, as the applicability of this procedural requirement can be relaxed by the Court wherever the interest of justice so justifies.
obiter: The threshold admissibility of an electronic evidence cannot be ruled out on any technicality if the same is relevant.
Reliability of a piece of evidence is a matter to be determined in the facts and circumstances of a fact situation.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The requirement to produce a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is not mandatory for the admissibility of electronic evidence when the party producing it is not in possession or control of the original device. In such situations, the court can relax the procedural requirement in the interest of justice, and the evidence can be proven by invoking other provisions like Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act.
legal_tests_applied: The applicability of the procedural requirement under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act of furnishing a certificate is to be applied only when such electronic evidence is produced by a person who is in a position to produce such a certificate, being in control of the said device.
why_respondent_won: A party who is not in possession of the device from which the document is produced cannot be required to produce a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act.

In a case where electronic evidence is produced by a party who is not in possession of a device, the applicability of Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act cannot be held to be excluded and the procedure under those sections can be invoked.

The threshold admissibility of an electronic evidence cannot be ruled out on any technicality if the same was relevant, as the reliability of the evidence is a separate matter to be determined in the facts and circumstances of the case.
policy_considerations: The applicability of the requirement of a certificate, being procedural, can be relaxed by the Court wherever the interest of justice so justifies.

To hold otherwise would result in a denial of justice to a person who is in possession of authentic evidence but cannot possibly secure the required certificate, leading to the evidence being kept out of consideration by the court.
